title: Jack of Hearts

image.credit: collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A colorful, fragmented painting that breaks a playing-card figure into angular shapes and patches of color, in the style of Cubism.

source.museum: collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, years, medium, movement label); collection not stated on the page

context: An oil painting on canvas by the Russian artist Olga Rozanova, dated 1912 to 1915 on its source page, which labels it Cubist. Its title names a playing card, and the page does not state its collection.

descriptions.k: This is a playing card jack, but it is made of broken shapes. Can you find a face or a heart? Which colors do you see?
descriptions.g12: Olga Rozanova painted a jack from a deck of cards. She broke him into many shapes and bright pieces, like a puzzle. Can you find a heart? Which pieces make the jack?
descriptions.g35: Olga Rozanova painted Jack of Hearts between 1912 and 1915. Like a Cubist painter, she breaks the figure into angled pieces so you see parts from different angles at once. A playing card is a flat picture already. How does the painting turn this card into something new to puzzle out?
descriptions.g68: Jack of Hearts (1912-1915) by Olga Rozanova is a Cubist oil painting that fragments a playing-card figure into angular planes and color patches. The subject is already a flat, patterned image, which suits the style. How do overlapping shapes make you piece together the figure, and what does that slow looking teach?
descriptions.g910: Rozanova's Jack of Hearts (1912-1915) adapts Cubist fragmentation to a deliberately flat subject, a playing card. This was a period when Russian artists absorbed and reworked Cubism. Where do figure and pattern merge? How does the broken surface ask you to construct the image yourself, and why might a card be a clever choice?
descriptions.g1112: Jack of Hearts (1912-1915) shows Olga Rozanova working in a Cubist idiom during a time of fast experiment among Russian avant-garde artists. A playing card, an image designed to be read quickly and symmetrically, is dismantled into planes. How might the painting be read as play, as a test of representation, or as a step toward abstraction, and what evidence limits each reading?

g1112.technique: How does the fragmented technique engage the viewer as a collaborator in constructing the image?

teacherNote.context: A 1912 to 1915 oil painting by the Russian artist Olga Rozanova, labeled Cubist on its source page. It breaks a playing-card figure into angular fragments; the page does not state the collection.
directions: Have students draw a simple card figure, cut it into angular pieces and reassemble it with small gaps, then compare results.
Ask students to describe how they found the heart or face, and discuss how the brain fills gaps.
Discuss why artists might choose everyday objects like cards as subjects.
